title: Azure Cosmos DB Pricing: A 2026 Guide to Costs
summary: Azure Cosmos DB pricing combines request units and storage; capacity mode determines costs. Compare what each billing approach actually charges.
body_markdown:
## Building Cosmos DB spend alerts with an Activepieces workflow


Even the cheaper mode won't help if nobody sees the bill drifting. The first question is who gets told when it does. Azure can raise the alarm; it won't decide who owns the response.


### What Azure already gives you for alerts


Azure covers detection with three built-in tools. Cost Management budgets let you set a spend threshold on a subscription, resource group or single account, and notify when actual or forecast spend crosses it.


That means you hear about a runaway bill before the invoice, not after.


Anomaly alerts flag spend that departs from your recent pattern, which catches the case where no fixed threshold was ever set.


Azure Monitor alerts watch the account's metrics, most usefully request unit consumption and throttled requests (HTTP 429). A rising consumption line tells you a query or a new feature is costing more per call.


A burst of 429s tells you the opposite problem: you're under-provisioned and users are being refused.


The gap is delivery. These alerts land in an action group, which sends email or calls a webhook to whoever is listed.


If that list is one person who has since changed roles, the alert goes to nobody in particular, and you find out from a customer.


### Routing alerts when spending hits limits


An Activepieces flow with a schedule trigger can take spend figures from your cost export or an API call, branch on a threshold, and message Slack or email through its 747 integrations, which means almost any notification system is likely already wired in; if a system has no integration, generate one with AI and add it privately.


It is a monitoring add-on, not an answer to pricing, and it puts an owner behind each alert.


The flow below is a long, general-purpose example, not a Cosmos DB template.


It shows a schedule trigger feeding a Google Sheets lookup, a loop, a date step, an HTTP request, two AI steps, a sheet insert, a router with a Branch 1 and an Otherwise path, and a Gmail send step, meaning this is a multi-step orchestration with branching logic and external service integrations.


Take from it the shape rather than the length: a scheduled pull, a decision, and a message to a named person.


Applied here, a scheduled workflow can call the Azure cost or metrics endpoints over HTTP and compare the result with a threshold kept in a sheet.


The router can then send budget breaches to a ticket, throttling spikes to the on-call channel in Slack, and routine summaries to email. A run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so a daily check fits inside the Free plan's 1,000 monthly credits.


Describe that check in the built-in chat and what it publishes is a live flow in your account, with a run trace that shows exactly what happened at each step, from the Azure call to the Slack post.


The sheet doubles as the record of who owns each account.


None of this changes what Cosmos DB charges. It shortens the time between a bad spend pattern and a person acting on it.
